findings.explanation: high confidence.  Witness: Whenever \dim H_0^{i, n-1-i} \geq 2, there exist linearly independent polynomials g^{(1)}, g^{(2)} such that neither f \cdot g^{(1)} nor f \cdot g^{(2)} lies in \mathrm{Jac}(G). Theorem 2.3 asserts that the conjugate is proportional to g for any such choice, which would imply that two linearly independent classes both equal the complex conjugate of \varphi_{\mathbb{C}}([y^i f]), a contradiction. In general, pairing against a single element f only gives one linear condition on an element of H_0^{i, n-1-i}, which does not uniquely determine it when the dimension is greater than 1; one must invert the full intersection/period matrix on the Hodge component rather than choosing an arbitrary polynomial g.

findings.explanation: high confidence.  Witness: For dimension of H_0^{n-1-i, i} greater than 1, the pairing R(y^i f_{j_i}, y^{n-1-i} h) = U_{k,\gamma} only specifies a single scalar condition on h, which is an affine hyperplane of elements rather than uniquely determining the class \overline{\phi_C([y^i f_{j_i}])}. An arbitrary choice of g_{j_i} in (2.10) will not span the complex conjugate class in general; the full intersection matrix on a basis of the Hodge component is required to invert the pairing and determine the conjugate class uniquely in higher dimensions. Consequently, Corollary 2.7 also fails when |I_i| > 1 because w_{j_i} is not in general an invariant class under complex conjugation when \tilde{f}_{j_i} is not the true complex conjugate of f_{j_i} modulo the Jacobian ideal.
